title: Natural Domains of Three Formulas
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: Define what a natural domain is, then find the natural domains of f(x) = sqrt(x), g(x) = 1/(x^2 - 4), and h(x) = x/(x^2 + 1).
finalAnswer: Natural domains: $\sqrt{x}$ on $[0, \infty)$; $\dfrac{1}{x^2-4}$ on $\{x : x \ne \pm 2\}$; $\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}$ on $(-\infty, \infty)$.

steps.title: Define the Natural Domain
steps.mathExpression: D_{\text{natural}} = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) \text{ is defined by the formula}\}
steps.explanation: When a function is given only by a formula with no domain stated, we assume the largest set of real numbers on which the formula makes sense. Two usual culprits restrict this set: even roots of negative quantities and division by zero.
steps.why: The definition tells you exactly which algebraic checks to run.

steps.title: Rule Out Negative Radicands
steps.explanation: For f(x) = sqrt(x), the square root requires a nonnegative radicand, so the natural domain is [0, infinity).
steps.why: Even roots of negative numbers are undefined in the real number system.

steps.title: Rule Out Zero Denominators
steps.explanation: For g(x) = 1/(x^2 - 4), the denominator vanishes at x = 2 and x = -2, so the natural domain is all reals except ±2. For h(x) = x/(x^2 + 1), the denominator satisfies x^2 + 1 >= 1 and never vanishes, so the natural domain is all real numbers.
steps.why: Factorizing the denominator exposes exactly which points must be removed, while a strictly positive denominator removes none.
